article_markdown:
---
title: "How to Turn Your Work Notes into a Clear AI Brief in Minutes"
subtitle: "Step-by-step: turn messy meeting notes, scattered data, and rough sketches into polished briefs, memos, and specs using ChatGPT."
category: "how-to"
audience: "both"
read_time_minutes: 9
tags: ["chatgpt-work", "data-briefs", "professional-writing", "ai-productivity"]
---

> **In short:** This guide walks you through four real workflows in ChatGPT — meeting notes into a brief, raw data into a KPI memo, a sketch into a dashboard spec, and a quick-start practice round. Each step shows exactly where to click, what to paste, and what a working prompt looks like.

You walk out of a meeting with a notepad full of half-finished bullets, a long email thread on your phone, and two voice memos you forgot existed. By lunch, your manager wants a one-page brief. This guide shows you how to feed that messy input into ChatGPT and get back a clean, structured document you can actually send.

Before we start, here's what you'll need:

- **A ChatGPT account** (free tier works for the steps below; ChatGPT Plus is faster for long inputs but not required)
- **A web browser** or the official ChatGPT mobile app (iOS or Android)
- **Your raw notes** — typed bullets, a copied email thread, a short transcript, or a photo of a whiteboard
- **About 10–15 minutes** for your first run-through

## Step 1 — Open a new chat and paste in your raw notes

Open **chat.openai.com** in your browser (or open the ChatGPT app and tap the **"New chat"** pencil icon at the top). You'll see an empty text box at the bottom of the screen with a send arrow on the right.

Copy your notes from wherever they live — a Google Doc, an email, your phone's notes app — and paste them straight into the text box. Don't clean them up first. The whole point is that the AI handles the mess.

After you paste, you'll see your notes appear in a gray message bubble above the text box. The text box is now empty and ready for your instruction.

💬 Example line to copy: *"Here are my raw meeting notes. Please don't rewrite yet — just confirm you've received them and tell me how many words I pasted."*

**You'll know it worked when** ChatGPT responds with a short message acknowledging the text and (usually) a word or character count.

## Step 2 — Ask ChatGPT to turn the notes into a structured brief

In the same chat, type a new instruction below the assistant's previous reply. The text box is still at the bottom of the screen. Press **Enter** to send.

Tell the AI what kind of document you want and what sections it should include. Be specific about the topic so it doesn't drift into generic business language.

After you send, you'll see a new assistant message appear with headings, bullet points, and short paragraphs — the brief in finished form.

💬 Example line to copy:

> *"Turn these notes into a root-cause brief. The main issue is customer churn last quarter. Please include: (1) the primary issue, (2) at least three contributing factors, (3) two immediate actions, and (4) one KPI to track. Keep it under 400 words."*

**You'll know it worked when** the response has clear headings matching your four numbered requests, not a single wall of text.

## Step 3 — Turn raw data into a KPI memo

Start a fresh chat by clicking **"New chat"** at the top-left of the sidebar (web) or tapping the pencil icon again (mobile). A blank conversation helps the AI focus on this specific task without mixing in old context.

Paste a small table or a few rows of numbers directly into the text box. If your data is in a spreadsheet, copy 10–20 representative rows — you don't need to paste thousands. Below the data, add one sentence explaining what the numbers represent (sales, traffic, support tickets, etc.).

You'll see two stacked bubbles: your data on top, then your instruction. The reply will arrive as a short memo with metric names, plain-language explanations, and a recommendation.

💬 Example line to copy:

> *"Above is monthly sales data for our team. Write a KPI memo that: (1) names the top 3 metrics with the biggest change this month, (2) explains in plain English why each might have changed, and (3) recommends one next step. Use bullet points."*

**You'll know it worked when** the memo names specific numbers from your paste (not made-up figures) and ends with a concrete "next step" sentence.

## Step 4 — Turn a rough sketch into a dashboard specification

Open a new chat the same way as Step 3. If your sketch is on paper, snap a photo and use the **attachment** (paperclip) icon on the left of the text box to upload it. If it's a quick list in your notes app, just paste the bullet points instead.

After you attach or paste, type your instruction in the same text box and send. ChatGPT will read the image or the bullets and reply with a structured spec.

You'll see the uploaded image as a small thumbnail above your message, and the reply below it as a multi-section document with a clear purpose, metric definitions, suggested chart types, and a data-source list.

💬 Example line to copy:

> *"I've pasted a rough sketch for a 'Customer Support Performance' dashboard. Please turn it into a detailed spec that includes: (1) the dashboard's purpose, (2) definitions for each metric, (3) suggested visualisations like line graph or bar chart for each metric, and (4) a list of required data sources."*

**You'll know it worked when** each metric from your sketch appears in the spec with its own definition and a named chart type beside it.

## Step 5 — Refine the output until it sounds like you

Stay in the same chat. Below the assistant's last reply, type a short follow-up such as *"Make it more concise"*, *"Use a more formal tone"*, or *"Add a one-sentence summary at the top"*. Press **Enter**.

You'll see the assistant replace the previous document with a new version that reflects your edit. The old version stays visible above it, so you can compare.

💬 Example line to copy: *"Shorter version please — 150 words max, and start with a one-sentence summary in bold."*

**You'll know it worked when** the new reply is visibly shorter (or differently toned) than the previous one, and the changes match exactly what you asked for.

## Step 6 — Copy the finished document into your work tool

Highlight the assistant's final reply by clicking at the start and dragging to the end. Right-click (or long-press on mobile) and choose **"Copy"**. Then open your email, Google Doc, or Slack and paste.

You'll see your formatted brief, memo, or spec appear with all the headings and bullets intact.

💬 Example line to copy (sent to the AI in a new chat, as practice): *"Summarize the email I pasted above into three bullet points I can paste into Slack."*

**You'll know it worked when** the text lands in your destination tool formatted the way you want, with no broken headings or stray code.

## Common mistakes

- **Pasting sensitive or private data without thinking.** Fix: remove client names, employee IDs, or financial figures before you paste, or replace them with placeholders like "[Client A]" and put the real names back in the final document yourself.
- **Writing vague prompts like "make this better."** Fix: name the document type ("memo", "brief", "spec"), the audience ("my manager", "the analytics team"), and any limits ("under 300 words", "bullet points only").
- **Starting a new chat for every small tweak.** Fix: stay in the same chat for follow-up edits — the AI remembers the conversation, which makes refinements much faster.
- **Trusting every number in the output.** Fix: if you asked for a KPI memo, double-check that the numbers in the reply actually came from your pasted data, not invented values. The AI can sometimes fill gaps with plausible-sounding figures.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** The same workflow works for non-work stuff. Paste a jumble of holiday planning notes and ask for a day-by-day itinerary, or paste a messy shopping list and ask for it grouped by store aisle.
- **For your work:** This pattern — paste raw input, ask for a specific structure, then refine — turns 30–60 minutes of document drafting into about 5 minutes of prompting and editing. You'll still review every line before sending.
- **If you're just getting started:** Try Step 6's practice prompt first. Copy one short email you received, paste it into a new chat, and ask for three bullet points. Once that feels easy, move up to Step 1 with your real meeting notes.
